title: How London's Great Stink Built Its Sewers
topic: Why the Great Stink of 1858 forced London to build sewers

lines: A worker spread lime across Thames mud while London choked on sewage.
The river had become London's open drain.
The lime worker returned at low tide, day after day.
Earlier sewer plans had been ignored because the costs were too high.
Now the stink could no longer be ignored.
Queen Victoria and Prince Albert tried a pleasure cruise on the Thames.
Queen Victoria and Prince Albert returned to shore within minutes.
The press named it the Great Stink.
Members of Parliament fled the Commons chamber.
You see, it was like a hot, full rubbish bin in a sealed room.
The worker could hide the smell, but not the waste.
Londoners feared the stench would spread cholera.
London's old sewers emptied straight into the Thames.
More people and flushing toilets sent more waste into broken pipes.
Hot, dry weather dropped the river level and left raw sewage on the banks.
Joseph Bazalgette built sloping sewers that carried waste east, beyond the city.
Pumping stations lifted sewage into higher pipes.
But bad air wasn't the killer. Contaminated water was.
The stench simply forced Parliament to act.
Those sewers still carry waste for over nine million Londoners.

claims.claim: Men were employed spreading lime onto the Thames foreshore at low tide to fight the smell, at a cost of £1,500 per week.
Queen Victoria and Prince Albert attempted a pleasure cruise on the Thames but returned to shore within a few minutes because the smell was so terrible.
The press called the event the Great Stink, and Parliament was compelled to legislate by the force of the stench.
The stink drove Members of Parliament from the House of Commons chamber.
London's ageing, inadequate sewers emptied directly into the Thames, and hot, dry weather in 1858 lowered the river level so raw effluent remained on the banks.
Joseph Bazalgette's accepted plan moved effluent eastwards along interconnecting sewers sloped toward outfalls beyond the metropolitan area, with pumping stations lifting sewage into higher pipes.
Earlier proposals to modernise London's sewers were neglected because of their costs, and after the Great Stink Parliament gave Bazalgette responsibility for a modern system.
Dr John Snow correctly diagnosed contaminated water as the way cholera spread in 1849, but bad air was blamed until the 1866 outbreak.
Bazalgette's sewer system still operates in the 21st century, serving a city grown to over nine million people.
